title: Trial Dedicated Sizing & Autoscale Retrospective
summary: Week 3 POC check-in focused on Dedicated sizing adjustments after observed burst behavior during end-of-day batch scoring. Reviewed autoscale thresholds, prewarm strategies, and KV cache warm-up; agreed to run two targeted load tests and adjust canary policy. Action items include finalizing CPU/GPU mix for burst nodes, schedule perf tests, and send updated cost estimate and policy doc.
topics: observed burst pattern and root cause
cost vs latency tradeoffs for burst nodes
action_items: Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE): produce a proposed autoscale policy YAML and node-type recommendation by 2026-04-13
Roberto Diaz (Helixa): share recent end-of-day request histogram + sample trace files by 2026-04-11
Maya Patel (AE): update commercial estimate with burst pricing and send by 2026-04-12
Alex Park (Helixa SRE): run the two load tests provided in the plan and post results to the shared sheet by 2026-04-16
next_steps: Redwood to deliver autoscale policy + prewarm playbook
Helixa to run test harness and validate cold start window
Align on final Dedicated sizing after test results (decision meeting week of 2026-04-20)
Exchange security/access notes for private cluster benchmark creds
header:
Date: 2026-04-09
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Tasha Reed (Redwood CSM), Sara Nguyen (Helixa Head of ML), Roberto Diaz (Helixa Platform Eng), Priya Menon (Helixa CTO), Alex Park (Helixa SRE)
Recording ID: zoom.us/rec/abcd1234
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Okay, hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. This is week three of the Helixa Dedicated trial, and main goals for today are to review the burst incident on Thursday, look at autoscale settings, and land on a test plan.
[00:14] Sara (Helixa): Thanks, Maya. Yep, we had two end-of-day spikes where latency jumped to p95 ~1.8s and p99 touched 5.2s. It felt like cache misses amplified by concurrent cold-shots — uh, cold starts.
[00:28] Liam (Redwood SE): Right, from the traces we saw a lot of model loading activity at the same time. There were KV cache miss patterns — the cache wasn't fully populated across the new nodes during the burst. Also saw a handful of small OOM logs on one of the older GPUs.
[00:45] Roberto (Helixa): Clarify, when you say "prewarm," do you mean separate warm nodes or a prewarm job that loads KV and token cache?
[00:54] Liam: Both are valid. Our recommendation usually is to combine a small prewarm pool that stays hot for the expected burst window plus a short-lived prewarm job that warms the KV cache when scale events happen. That reduces the cold-window to sub-200ms for most requests.
[01:10] Priya (CTO): I want to be clear on cost. If we keep a prewarm pool for spikes, how much of our committed capacity are we wasting?
[01:18] Maya: Good question. We'll show two cost scenarios — minimal prewarm (single small node) vs. heavier prewarm (2-3 nodes); the heavier prewarm buys you lower p99 but increases effective hourly cost. We'll attach an updated cost table after this call.
[01:34] Alex (SRE): The spikes are predictable — end of day batch scoring and ad-hoc user queries — maybe a 10-12 minute window. Is it worth configuring a time-based autoscale rule?
[01:45] Liam: Absolutely. We can make a hybrid autoscale policy: schedule-based scaling for the known window + reactive scaling for unpredicted load. Also recommend a higher scale step (bigger ramp) during scheduled windows.
[02:00] Sara: We saw about 300 concurrent sessions at peak — mostly short chat completions for insights. Average seq length was 180 tokens.
[02:08] Liam: That seq distribution matters for batching strategy. If average is 180, we can tune batch size and model variant to optimize throughput. For Dedicated, we proposed the g5x2-like nodes (example) with 4 replicas, but maybe we need 6 for bursts.
[02:26] Roberts (note: transcription error, likely Roberto): —
[02:30] Maya: One other weirdness: during the spike there was a routing fallback to the hosted model in another region for around 2 minutes. That may have affected end-to-end latency. We're going to look at the routing logs.
[02:44] Priya: Is fallback expected? We pinned the model version.
[02:48] Liam: Fallback is policy-driven — when Dedicated capacity was exhausted, the control plane triggered fallback to a compatible model in hosted to avoid errors. It preserves availability but can increase latency and cost. We'll share the fallback timeline with timestamps.
[03:05] Alex: For the node sizing, can we mix GPU types so the burst uses quantized variants on cheaper devices?
[03:13] Liam: Yes, heterogeneous pools are supported. You can route low-latency, high-cost traffic to the high-end GPUs and background scoring to quantized variants on cheaper GPUs. But watch out for model variant compatibility and cold-start differences.
[03:30] Sara: Ok, what's the plan for the two tests you mentioned?
[03:34] Liam: Test A: Recreate the end-of-day spike with scheduled scaled-up baseline + no prewarm to measure cold-start penalty. Test B: Same spike but with prewarm pool + KV cache preloading to measure improvement. Each test will run three times and we capture p50/p95/p99, error rate, and token cost.
[03:55] Roberto: We'll need the exact test harness and k6 script. Can you drop it in the shared folder?
[04:02] Maya: Yes, we'll upload the harness, a small guide, and the sample makefile. We'll also include the exact curl payloads and the sample trace collector settings.
[04:12] Priya: One operational question: how long does it typically take to bring up extra nodes in Dedicated? We saw about a 45s median in Thursday's event.
[04:20] Liam: That sounds like typical instance spin-up + model load. With prewarm you reduce that to the model load time only, which in your case is around 12-18s for the full model. If we use a smaller quantized variant on burst nodes the load can be 4-6s.
[04:38] Sara: Any risk with prewarming from a security perspective? We don't want unencrypted cache sitting around.
[04:45] Tasha (Redwood CSM): All prewarm work occurs inside the customer's Dedicated cluster with your CMK; logs and cache are under customer control. We can consult the security pack and add notes on cache lifecycle.
[04:58] Alex: Great. Also, on the autoscale policy, what metric should we use? RPS? GPU util? Latency?
[05:05] Liam: We prefer a two-tier metric: GPU util or queued requests for reactive scale, with an SLO-based guard using p95 latency. For schedule-based steps, time windows plus predictive headroom works well.
[05:20] Sara: During the spike we saw very low GPU util on some nodes despite queue buildup — was that because requests were unevenly routed?
[05:27] Liam: It looked like the batcher wasn't filling ideally due to short-lived sessions and slight sequence length variance. We'll recommend modifying batch thresholds and enabling a tiny batching delay to increase packing density during the burst window. That trades a few ms for a big win on throughput/cost.
[05:48] Priya: Let's talk about the decision criteria after the tests. We have an internal cost threshold and a latency SLO (p95 < 750ms). If prewarm gets us under that at a cost within 12% of baseline, we prefer it.
[06:02] Maya: Noted. We'll model those scenarios in the cost spreadsheet.
[06:08] Roberto: Regarding the canary rollout — if we change autoscale policy, how do we test safely?
[06:14] Liam: Canary policy: route a small fraction (5-10%) of traffic to the new policy for the first 30 minutes, monitor latency/error rate. If okay, ramp to 50% then full. We'll give the exact A/B YAML.
[06:27] Sara: Are there existing policies in the console we can copy?
[06:30] Tasha: Yes, we'll put a template into the project workspace — "scheduled-plus-reactive".
[06:36] Alex: For the KV cache warm-up, how do you recommend prepopulating? We have a corpus of hot prefixes.
[06:42] Liam: We'll provide a loader: warm the top 5k prefixes via a synthetic batch job that touches KV entries. We'll also persist hot shards to speed rehydration. Note: it depends on your model's cache sharding strategy.
[06:55] Priya: Who owns the security review for running the loader?
[06:58] Tasha: Helixa will approve the job; Redwood will provide the script and run it under your service account, or you can run it in your environment — whichever you prefer.
[07:09] Maya: Okay, let's talk timeline. If Roberto can share histograms by Sunday, Liam can push the YAML Monday, and Maya will update cost on Monday as well, we can run Test A on Wednesday and Test B on Thursday. Does that work?
[07:23] Roberto: Yes, that works for us.
[07:26] Alex: One more thing — we saw one request that triggered a fallback to hosted because the control plane thought the Dedicated model was incompatible. Is that a model ABI mismatch?
[07:36] Liam: Likely a minor variant flag mismatch between the pinned model and the newer compatible variant. We'll check the deployment logs; this can be fixed by aligning model tags in the pin. We'll add that to the post-mortem.
[07:48] Sara: From our side, please mark p99 before and after so we can judge absolute improvements.
[07:52] Liam: Will do. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and cost per 1k tokens.
[07:58] Priya: Any concerns about sustained burst capacity if we see simultaneous external events?
[08:03] Liam: Sustained large bursts require reserved burst capacity or negotiated burst limits. We can include burst reservations in the Dedicated contract for critical windows. That is an optional contract add-on.
[08:16] Maya: On pricing, we'll separate base Dedicated commit cost from optional burst reservation pricing and show effective per-token cost for each test run.
[08:26] Tasha: I'm uploading a checklist now to the shared drive: items for Helixa to provide, and items Redwood will supply.
[08:34] Maya: Quick recap so everyone's aligned — 1) Redwood to deliver autoscale policy YAML + prewarm playbook by 2026-04-13; 2) Helixa to share histograms and traces by 2026-04-11; 3) Maya to send updated cost estimate by 2026-04-12; 4) Helixa to run Test A & B and post results by 2026-04-16. Any additions?
[08:58] Priya: Add a decision meeting in week of 2026-04-20.
[09:02] Maya: Noted — I'll calendar that.
[09:05] Sara: Thanks, team. This is productive.
[09:08] Liam: One final note — we'll also run a tiny bench that simulates the fallback path so we have a baseline for hosted fallback latency.
[09:16] Roberto: Good idea.
[09:18] Maya: Alright, we're at time. We'll follow up with the artifacts and the drive links. Thanks everyone, see you next week.
[09:25] End of recording (approx 55 minutes).
